subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 16. In this unit you move beyond simply collecting numbers and drawing graphs. You will learn to interpret data – to say what it actually means – and to discuss results the way a real statistician does: carefully, honestly, and with a critical eye. Every day, people around you are handed statistics. A shopkeeper in Mogadishu hears that prices rose “on average” last month. A football fan reads that one striker “scores more consistently” than another. A news report claims that “9 out of 10 people prefer” a certain brand. Behind every one of those claims sits data that someone chose to summarise in a particular way. Your job this unit is to look behind the claim.

outcomes: Calculate and interpret the mean, median and mode, and choose the most suitable average for a data set.
Measure the spread of data using the range and the interquartile range (IQR).
Compare two distributions by referring to an average and a measure of spread, in a written sentence.
Draw and interpret a scatter graph, and describe the correlation as positive, negative or none, and as strong or weak.

Recognise misleading graphs, biased samples and unfair averages, and critique statistical claims.
Write a clear, evidence-based conclusion that answers a question and states its own limitations.

concepts.title: Averages – Choosing the Right One
concepts.explanation:
An average is a single number that stands in for a whole set of values – a typical value. There are three averages you must know, and the skill in Stage 8 is not just calculating them but choosing the one that describes the data most fairly.

The mean is the total of all the values divided by how many values there are. Suppose seven students at Nuur Academy score 78, 82, 85, 79, 91, 88, 76 on a test. The mean is (78 + 82 + 85 + 79 + 91 + 88 + 76) ÷ 7 = 579 ÷ 7 = 82.7. The mean uses every single value, which is its strength. But that is also its weakness: one unusual value can drag it a long way. If one student had scored 12 instead of 76, the mean would crash, even though most students did well.

The median is the middle value once the data is placed in order. Ordering the same scores gives 76, 78, 79, 82, 85, 88, 91, so the median is 82. When there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values. The median’s great strength is that it is barely affected by an extreme value – it just reports the middle, no matter how odd the ends are. This is why the median is the fairer average for things like incomes or house prices, where a few very large values would distort the mean.

The mode is the value that appears most often. For the heights (cm) 165, 167, 165, 170, 168, 165, 172, the mode is 165 because it appears three times. A set can have no mode, one mode, or several modes. The mode is the only average that works for categories that are not numbers at all – you cannot take the mean of ‘favourite fruit’, but you can say the mode is mango.
concepts.example: So which do you choose? Ask what the data is like. If the values are fairly even with no extreme outlier, the mean is usually best because it uses all the information. If there is an outlier or the data is skewed, the median is fairer. If the data is categorical, or you want the most common choice, use the mode. Being able to justify your choice in a sentence – ‘I used the median because the £4,000 value is an outlier that would inflate the mean’ – is exactly the kind of statistical reasoning this unit rewards.

concepts.title: Spread – Range and the Interquartile Range
concepts.explanation:
An average tells you where the centre of the data sits, but it says nothing about how spread out the values are. Two footballers might both average 12 goals a season, yet one scores steadily each year while the other swings wildly between 2 and 25. To capture this, you need a measure of spread.

The simplest measure of spread is the range: the highest value minus the lowest. For the scores 76 to 91, the range is 91 − 76 = 15. The range is quick to find, but it has a serious flaw: it depends only on the two most extreme values, so a single outlier can make the spread look enormous when almost all the data is actually tightly packed.

The interquartile range (IQR) fixes this. First you find the quartiles, which split the ordered data into four equal parts. Q1 (the lower quartile) has one quarter of the data below it; Q2 is the median; Q3 (the upper quartile) has three quarters below it. The IQR is then Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of the data. Because it throws away the extreme quarter at each end, the IQR is not fooled by outliers – it describes where the bulk of the data lives.

Let us find the IQR for these eleven values: 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28, 30, 35, 38, 42 (already in order). The median (Q2) is the 6th value, 25. The lower half is 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, and its middle value is 18, so Q1 = 18. The upper half is 28, 30, 35, 38, 42, and its middle value is 35, so Q3 = 35. Therefore IQR = 35 − 18 = 17. Compare this with the range, 42 − 12 = 30. The IQR of 17 tells us the central half of the data is packed more tightly than the full range suggests.
concepts.example: A small measure of spread means the data is consistent (values close together); a large measure means the data is variable (values spread out). When you describe spread, always say what it means in the context: ‘the smaller IQR shows Class B’s marks were more consistent’ tells the reader something useful, whereas ‘the IQR is 17’ on its own does not.

concepts.title: Comparing Two Distributions
concepts.explanation:
A distribution is the whole picture of how a set of values is spread out. One of the most important skills in this unit is comparing two distributions – two classes, two players, two markets – and saying which is ‘better’ or how they differ. The golden rule is this: always compare an average AND a measure of spread, and always write your comparison in context. One number is never enough.

Why both? Imagine two Stage 8 classes sit the same maths test. Class A has a median of 62 and an IQR of 8. Class B has a median of 62 and an IQR of 20. Their averages are identical, so if you only reported the median you would say the classes performed ‘the same’. But the spreads tell a completely different story. Class A’s marks are bunched close to 62 – the class is consistent, and the teaching reached everyone. Class B’s marks are scattered widely – some students did very well while others struggled badly. A good comparison sentence would be: ‘Both classes have the same median mark of 62, but Class A has a much smaller IQR, so Class A’s results are more consistent while Class B has a wider spread of ability.’

Now the other case: same spread, different centre. Suppose Hassan and Yusuf both play in the school football team. Over ten matches Hassan’s pass-completion has a median of 70% with an IQR of 6, and Yusuf’s has a median of 82% with an IQR of 6. Their consistency is the same, but Yusuf’s typical performance is higher. The comparison: ‘Yusuf has a higher median completion rate than Hassan, and since both have the same IQR they are equally consistent, so Yusuf is the stronger passer overall.’

Statisticians often use box plots to compare distributions at a glance. A box plot is drawn from the five-number summary: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. The box stretches from Q1 to Q3 (so its width shows the IQR), a line inside marks the median, and ‘whiskers’ reach out to the minimum and maximum. When two box plots are stacked one above the other on the same scale, you can instantly see which has the higher median (compare the middle lines), which is more spread out (compare the box widths), and whether either is skewed (is the median line in the middle of its box, or pushed to one side?).
concepts.example: When you compare using box plots, read them like sentences. A box that sits further to the right has generally higher values. A wider box means a larger IQR and more variability. If the median line is closer to Q1 than to Q3, more of the data is bunched at the lower end, so the distribution is skewed towards the higher values. Always translate what you see back into the real situation: ‘the water-collection times for the near well have a lower median and a narrower box, so that well is both quicker and more predictable than the far well.’

concepts.title: Scatter Graphs and Correlation
concepts.explanation:
So far we have looked at one quantity at a time. A scatter graph lets you explore whether two quantities are related. You collect pairs of measurements – for each person, or day, or animal, you record two things – and plot each pair as a single point, with one variable on the x-axis and the other on the y-axis.

For example, suppose you record the height and shoe size of six people: heights 155, 160, 165, 170, 175, 180 cm and shoe sizes 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. Plotting the points (155, 6), (160, 7), (165, 8) and so on, you would see the dots climbing steadily from bottom-left to top-right. That upward trend is a sign of a relationship between height and shoe size.

The pattern the points make is called correlation. There are three basic kinds:

Positive correlation: as one variable increases, the other tends to increase. The points slope upward from left to right. Example: hours revised and test score.

Negative correlation: as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease. The points slope downward from left to right. Example: temperature and sales of hot tea.

No correlation: there is no clear pattern; the points are scattered with no trend. Example: a student’s shoe size and their exam mark.

Correlation also has a strength. If the points lie very close to a straight line, the correlation is strong; if they show a trend but are quite scattered, it is weak; if they fall exactly on a line, it is perfect (rare in real data). So a full description of a scatter graph names both the direction and the strength: ‘there is a strong positive correlation between revision time and test score’ or ‘there is a weak negative correlation between age of a phone and its resale value’.

When there is correlation, you can draw a line of best fit: a single straight line that passes as close as possible to as many points as possible, with roughly equal numbers of points above and below it. A good line of best fit passes through or near the ‘mean point’ (the point whose coordinates are the mean of the x-values and the mean of the y-values). You do not simply join the first and last dots, and the line does not have to pass through the origin – you balance it through the whole cloud of points.
concepts.example: Once you have a line of best fit, you can make predictions. Reading a value from within the range of your data is called interpolation, and it is usually reliable. Reading a value from outside the range of your data is called extrapolation, and it is risky, because you are assuming the trend continues where you have no evidence. If Amina measured revision times between 1 and 5 hours, using her line to predict the score for 4 hours is fair interpolation; using it to predict the score for 20 hours of revision is extrapolation, and it may be nonsense – nobody can score more than 100%, and no one revises for twenty hours straight.

concepts.title: Correlation Is Not Causation
concepts.explanation:
This is one of the most important ideas in all of statistics, and one of the easiest to get wrong. Just because two things are correlated – they rise and fall together – does not mean that one causes the other. A relationship in the data is a clue, not a proof.

Here is the classic example. Across the year, ice-cream sales and cases of sunburn both go up and down together – a strong positive correlation. But ice cream does not cause sunburn, and sunburn does not cause people to buy ice cream. A third factor – hot, sunny weather – causes both. This hidden third factor is called a confounding variable. Whenever you see a correlation, your first question should be: could some other factor be driving both?

Consider a real-feeling case. A study finds that children who eat breakfast tend to score higher on tests – a positive correlation. It is tempting to conclude ‘breakfast causes higher marks’. But think of the confounders: children who eat breakfast may come from homes with more routine, more sleep, quieter study space, or more support with homework. Any of those could be the real cause, or part of it. The correlation is genuine and interesting, but it does not, by itself, prove that breakfast is the cause.
concepts.example: To move from correlation towards causation, statisticians look for more: a controlled experiment where only one factor is changed, a plausible mechanism explaining how one thing could cause the other, and results that repeat across different studies. Even then they stay careful. In this unit you are not expected to prove causation – you are expected to spot when someone else has claimed it too quickly, and to name a possible confounding variable. That single habit will protect you from a huge amount of misleading argument for the rest of your life.

concepts.title: Misleading Statistics and Unfair Samples
concepts.explanation:
Numbers can be used to inform you – or to fool you. Part of interpreting results is learning the common tricks, so you can spot them and refuse to be misled.

Misleading scales. The most common trick is a graph whose y-axis does not start at zero. Suppose a company’s sales rose from £100 million to £110 million – a modest 10% rise. If the y-axis starts at £95 million, the bar for £110 looks about three times taller than the bar for £100, making a small change appear dramatic. Always check where the axis starts before you believe a graph. Stretching or squashing an axis can make a steady trend look like a cliff or a flat line.

Cherry-picking. Someone shows only the time period that flatters their case – ‘sales have risen every month since June’ – while hiding that sales fell sharply from January to June. Choosing a convenient start point, or ignoring data that disagrees, is called cherry-picking. Always ask: what happened before the part they are showing me?

Unfair averages. Because the mean, median and mode can differ, a person can quote whichever average best supports their argument. If a business owner wants to look generous, they might quote the mean salary, which a few high-paid managers pull upward, rather than the median, which most workers are actually near. Always ask which average is being quoted and whether it is the fair one.
concepts.example: Biased samples. A conclusion about a whole population is only trustworthy if the sample it came from is representative. A survey about exercise habits conducted outside a gym will over-count fit, active people – that is selection bias. An online poll only reaches people who chose to respond, who often hold stronger opinions – voluntary-response bias. Leading questions like ‘Don’t you agree that…?’ nudge people toward a particular answer – response bias. To reduce bias you use fair sampling (ideally random), a large enough sample, and neutral question wording. When you read any statistic, ask: who was asked, how many, and how were they chosen?

methods.title: How to find the interquartile range
steps: Put all the data in order from smallest to largest.
Find the median (Q2) — the middle value.
Find Q1, the median of the lower half, and Q3, the median of the upper half.
Calculate IQR = Q3 − Q1.

methods.title: How to compare two distributions
methods.example: Class A: median 64, IQR 6. Class B: median 58, IQR 15. Compare the two classes’ test performance.
steps: Find an average (usually the median) for each set.
Find a measure of spread (usually the IQR) for each set.
Check both measures use the same units so the comparison is fair.

methods.title: Compare the spreads: which is more consistent, and what does that mean?
methods.example: Class R: median 50, IQR 4. Class S: median 50, IQR 18. Write a full sentence comparing them.
steps: Write one sentence covering both, in context.
Compare the two spread values directly — the smaller spread is the more consistent set.
Check your sentence names both which set is more consistent and by how much.

methods.title: How to use a scatter graph
methods.example: Temperature (°C) and ice-cream sales at a beach stall over six days: (24, 30), (26, 38), (28, 45), (30, 52), (32, 60), (34, 66). Plot the points, describe the correlation, draw a line of best fit, and use it to predict sales at 29°C.
steps: Plot each pair of values as a point.
Describe the correlation: direction (positive/negative/none) and strength (strong/weak).
Draw a line of best fit balancing points above and below.
Predict by interpolation (inside the data — reliable) or note extrapolation (outside — risky).

methods.title: Describing correlation
methods.example: On a scatter graph of ‘hours of revision’ against ‘test score’, the points rise from bottom-left to top-right and lie fairly close to a straight line. Describe the correlation and what it means.
steps: The points slope upward and lie close to a line, so there is a strong positive correlation between revision time and test score.
In context: students who revised for longer tended to score higher marks.
(Remember: this is a link, not proof that revision alone causes the higher score.)

methods.title: Interpolation vs extrapolation
methods.example: Farah’s scatter graph covers revision times from 1 to 5 hours. She uses her line of best fit to predict the score for (a) 3 hours and (b) 12 hours. Which prediction is reliable?
steps: Prediction (a) at 3 hours is inside the data range (1 to 5 hours), so it is interpolation and is reliable.
Prediction (b) at 12 hours is outside the range, so it is extrapolation — unreliable, because there is no evidence the trend continues that far, and the score cannot exceed 100% anyway.
Check by confirming whether your x-value falls inside or outside the original data range before trusting the prediction.

workedExamples.title: Mean, median, mode and range
workedExamples.prompt: Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 15, 18, 22, 18, 25, 30, 18, 27.
workedExamples.solution: There are 8 values. Mean = (15 + 18 + 22 + 18 + 25 + 30 + 18 + 27) ÷ 8 = 173 ÷ 8 = 21.625. To find the median, order them: 15, 18, 18, 18, 22, 25, 27, 30. With 8 values the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th: (18 + 22) ÷ 2 = 20. The mode is 18 (it appears three times). The range is 30 − 15 = 15.

workedExamples.title: Which average is fairest?
workedExamples.prompt: A small workshop pays five workers 200, 220, 210, 230 and 900 shillings a day. Which average best describes a typical wage?
workedExamples.solution: The mean is (200 + 220 + 210 + 230 + 900) ÷ 5 = 1760 ÷ 5 = 352 shillings. But four of the five workers earn close to 200–230, and only one earns 900. Ordering the wages — 200, 210, 220, 230, 900 — the median is 220 shillings. The median is the fairer typical wage: the outlier of 900 pulls the mean far above what most workers actually earn.

workedExamples.title: Interquartile range
workedExamples.solution: There are 11 values in order. The median (Q2) is the 6th value, 25. The lower half (below the median) is 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, so Q1 = 18. The upper half is 28, 30, 35, 38, 42, so Q3 = 35. Therefore IQR = 35 − 18 = 17. This is smaller than the range (30), showing the middle half of the data is more tightly packed than the extremes suggest.

workedExamples.title: Comparing two distributions
workedExamples.prompt: Class A: median 64, IQR 6. Class B: median 58, IQR 15. Compare the two classes’ test performance.
workedExamples.solution: ‘Class A has a higher median (64 vs 58), so Class A performed better on average. Class A also has a smaller IQR (6 vs 15), so Class A’s marks are more consistent, while Class B’s marks are much more spread out.’ A full comparison names the average and the spread, both in context — that is what earns full marks.

In context: students who revised for longer tended to score higher marks. (Remember: this is a link, not proof that revision alone causes the higher score.)

workedExamples.title: Interpolation vs extrapolation
workedExamples.prompt: Farah’s scatter graph covers revision times from 1 to 5 hours. She uses her line of best fit to predict the score for (a) 3 hours and (b) 12 hours. Which prediction is reliable?
workedExamples.solution: Prediction (a) at 3 hours is inside the data range (1 to 5 hours), so it is interpolation and is reliable. Prediction (b) at 12 hours is outside the range, so it is extrapolation — unreliable, because there is no evidence the trend continues that far, and the score cannot exceed 100% anyway.

workedExamples.title: Correlation vs causation
workedExamples.prompt: A newspaper reports: ‘Towns with more mobile phones have more cases of illness — phones are making people sick.’ Critique this conclusion.
workedExamples.solution: The conclusion mistakes correlation for causation. A likely confounding variable is population size: bigger towns have more of everything — more phones and more illness cases — without one causing the other. A fair comparison would use rates (cases per 1000 people), not raw totals. So the newspaper’s claim is not supported by the evidence given.

workedExamples.title: Critiquing a claim
workedExamples.prompt: ‘A survey outside the Hargeisa sports stadium found that 95% of people exercise daily, so most people in the city are very active.’ What is wrong with this conclusion?
workedExamples.solution: The sample is biased. People outside a sports stadium are far more likely to exercise than the general public, so this is selection bias — the sample is not representative of the whole city. The 95% figure describes stadium-goers, not everyone. A fair study would sample people from many different places across the city, chosen at random.

workedExamples.solution: Both classes have the same IQR (6, equally consistent), but Class Q has the higher median (60 vs 48), so Class Q performed better on average.

workedExamples.solution: Both classes have the same median (50), but Class S has a much larger IQR (18 vs 4), so Class R is far more consistent while Class S is very spread out.

workedExamples.solution: Negative correlation: as a car’s age increases, its resale value tends to decrease, because older cars usually have higher mileage, more wear and outdated features. The relationship is likely fairly strong, though not perfect, since a car’s condition also affects its value.

workedExamples.title: Explain, with an example, the difference between…
workedExamples.prompt: Explain, with an example, the difference between interpolation and extrapolation.
workedExamples.solution: Interpolation is predicting a value that lies inside the range of the data you collected — this is usually reliable. Extrapolation is predicting a value outside that range — this is less reliable because there is no evidence the trend continues. For example, if revision time from 1 to 5 hours was recorded against test score, predicting the score for 3 hours of revision is interpolation, but predicting for 12 hours is extrapolation.

activities.title: Your Own Data Investigation
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and about 15 people to ask (family, friends, classmates).
steps: Choose a question with a number answer, e.g. ‘How many minutes do you walk to the library or school?’
Collect the data from at least 15 people and write it in a list.
Calculate the mean, median, mode and range.
Find Q1, Q3 and the IQR. Which measure of spread do you trust more, and why?
Write two sentences: one describing a typical value, one describing the spread – both in context.

activities.title: The Scatter-Graph Hunt
activities.materials: paper, ruler, and pairs of measurements you can collect.
steps: Pick two things you think might be related, e.g. a person’s height and their arm span, or hours slept and mood score out of 10.
Measure both for at least 10 people and record the pairs.
Plot the pairs as points on a scatter graph.
Describe the correlation (type and strength) and draw a sensible line of best fit.
Use your line to predict one value by interpolation – then discuss whether extrapolating far beyond your data would be safe.

activities.title: Spot the Misleading Graph (Media Game)
activities.materials: newspapers, adverts, or online articles with graphs and statistics.
steps: Collect three graphs or statistical claims from any source.
For each, check: does the y-axis start at zero? Which average is quoted? How big was the sample?
Decide whether each is fair or misleading, and explain how you could fix a misleading one.
Make a ‘Statistics Hall of Fame and Shame’ poster with your best and worst examples.
This trains the single most useful habit in the unit: never believing a graph until you have read its scale.

activities.title: The Correlation-or-Cause Debate
activities.materials: a partner, family member, or your AI tutor to debate with.
steps: Write five ‘A goes with B’ statements, e.g. ‘towns with more phones have more illness’.
For each, one person argues ‘A causes B’ and the other must find a confounding variable.
Award a point every time someone names a believable hidden third factor.
Discuss: which of your five statements might actually be causal, and how could you test it fairly?

activities.title: Compare Two Distributions (Group Task)
activities.materials: your data from Activity 1 and a classmate’s data on the same question (or a second data set you collect yourself if no classmate is available).
steps: Put both data sets side by side. Calculate the median and IQR for each.
Write a full comparison sentence using both an average and a spread, in context.
If you can, sketch two box plots on the same scale and check they agree with your sentence.
Discuss whether your two samples are big enough and fair enough to draw any real conclusion.

activities.title: Design a Fair Survey (Investigation)
steps: Choose a question people disagree about, e.g. ‘Should the school day start later?’
Write a leading version of the question, then rewrite it as a neutral one.
Decide who you would ask and how, to avoid selection bias – explain your sampling choice.
Predict how a biased sample might change your result, then (if you can) test it on two different groups.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity best showed you why spread matters as much as the average? When was it hardest to tell correlation from cause? Which misleading trick would fool most people you know? Share your thoughts with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Always Compare an Average AND a Spread
rules.text: A distribution is the whole picture of how a set of values is spread out. One of the most important skills in this unit is comparing two distributions – two classes, two players, two markets – and saying which is ‘better’ or how they differ. The golden rule is this: always compare an average AND a measure of spread, and always write your comparison in context. One number is never enough.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A report says: ‘Villages with more storks have more babies born, so storks bring babies.’ Identify the confounding variable and explain the real reason for the correlation.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The confounding variable is town/village size: larger settlements have more buildings (more stork nests) and more people (more babies). Storks do not cause births; population size drives both.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A company’s sales bar chart has a y-axis starting at 980 instead of 0, making a rise from 1000 to 1010 look enormous. Explain two things wrong with this and how to fix them.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Problems: the truncated y-axis exaggerates a tiny 1% rise, and a reader is misled into seeing a dramatic increase. Fix: start the axis at 0, or clearly mark an axis break, and label the true values.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Two goalkeepers each concede a mean of 1 goal per match. Keeper A has an IQR of 0; Keeper B has an IQR of 3. Which would you sign, and why? Justify your choice – there is no single correct answer.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Either answer is acceptable with justification: Keeper A (IQR 0) is perfectly consistent – you always know what to expect, which is useful in a tense match. Keeper B (IQR 3) is more variable – capable of outstanding games but also risky ones. A cautious manager might prefer Keeper A’s reliability; a manager chasing a win might gamble on Keeper B’s occasional brilliance.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Amina surveys people leaving the library and concludes ‘most young people love reading’. Explain the bias in her sample and describe a fairer method.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Amina’s sample is biased because she only asked people who were already leaving the library – they are far more likely to enjoy reading than the average young person. This is selection bias: the sample is not representative of all young people. A fairer method would be to survey a random sample of young people from many different places (school, home, online), not just library visitors.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Correlation Is Not Causation.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: This is one of the most important ideas in all of statistics, and one of the easiest to get wrong. Just because two things are correlated – they rise and fall together – does not mean that one causes the other. A relationship in the data is a clue, not a proof. Here is the classic example. Across the year, ice-cream sales and cases of sunburn both go up and down together – a strong positive correlation. But ice cream does not cause sunburn, and sunburn does not cause people to buy ice cream. A third factor – hot, sunny weather – causes both: more people buy ice cream AND more people get sunburnt on hot days. This hidden third factor is called a confounding variable, and it is why a correlation is always a clue, never proof, that one thing causes another.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Misleading Statistics and Unfair Samples.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Numbers can be used to inform you – or to fool you. Part of interpreting results is learning the common tricks, so you can spot them and refuse to be misled. Misleading scales. The most common trick is a graph whose y-axis does not start at zero. Suppose a company’s sales rose from £100 million to £110 million – a modest 10% rise. If the y-axis starts at £95 million, the bar for £110 looks about three times taller than the bar for £100, making a small change appear dramatic. Always check where the axis starts before trusting a graph. Other tricks include cherry-picking a flattering time period and quoting results from a biased sample as if they represent everyone. The habit that protects you from all of these: read the axis, check the sample, and ask what has been left out before you believe a claim.
